note: Animal signature/head rule, verb poses, 4-leg ears+horse, hair locks, bird
rationale: The most common failures are missing or misattached signature parts. Birds, the worst category, have no head, beak or tail because the only bird recipe is a tiny flying squiggle. Horse, cow and pig lose their ears and horns because the four-legged template left ears unspecified, so the drawer mirrored them onto the rump. The horse neck is pencil-thin and reads as a dinosaur, and the pig snout is lost against its pink head. People fail on identity: the long-hair oval hangs below the chin and reads as a beard for the girl and the princess. The girl, grandpa and pirate lack readable marks, and a multi-part bow failed to parse. Too-small subjects (flower, bird) slip through because scale=2 on a 110-tall recipe is still small. Action phrases, the worst category, draw a standing pose: the jumper stands beside the fence, the sleeper stands, the kite hangs at hand height, and a nest sits under its bird. A prop went off-page because local offsets were reused as paper anchors. Fixes: a general animal rule in How to draw well (separate head, face on the head, a bold signature part poking past the outline, gray outline for white things). A general verb rule covers jumping over, lying or sleeping, containers and kites. Anchors are paper points. The four-legged template now places explicit ears and horns on the head top and gives the horse a thick neck, long head and mane strip, the cow bold spots, the pig an outlined snout and a curly tail, and the giraffe long legs. The person gets long hair as side locks, a mirrored bow and a dress; the princess matches. Trait marks are sharpened. A real bird recipe replaces the flying squiggle. The scale tiers add 3x for tiny recipes. To pay for this, I cut the star, heart, sun, ball and table recipes (stamps and the Example cover them) and the broke and birthday beats.
